beats.text: Pots of honey, still good, sealed in tombs thousands of years old.
beats.note: Ancient Egyptian tombs in particular have turned up jars of honey that are millennia old and, once opened, still edible.

beats.text: Raw nectar is mostly water. Finished honey barely is.
beats.note: Bees fan the nectar with their wings until most of the moisture is gone, leaving too little water for bacteria to get a foothold.

beats.text: Honey is acidic, and it makes its own disinfectant.
beats.note: A pH of roughly 3 to 4.5 already kills off most microbes. An enzyme from the bees' own stomachs adds hydrogen peroxide on top, the same compound used to clean wounds.

beats.lead: This is not a new discovery
beats.text: Honey has been medicine for thousands of years.
beats.note: The earliest written use is on Sumerian clay tablets, where honey appears in roughly three in ten prescriptions. Egyptian physicians used it as a wound and eye ointment, because nothing could grow on it long enough to cause an infection.

beats.text: It only works sealed. Crack the jar and let the damp in, and even honey can finally spoil.

beats.line: The only food built to outlive the jar it's in.
